_comment: Single source of truth for the versions CI builds, tests and verifies against. Read by the
test-matrix job in .github/workflows/shared-test.yml, which composes the test legs and the
plugin-verification legs, and by .github/actions/setup-env, which fills any version input left
empty so the release/tag/build-plugin jobs need not restate the minimum supported platform.
Find available IDE versions at https://www.jetbrains.com/idea/download/other/ and
https://www.jetbrains.com/ruby/download/other/
Things you cannot tell from the values themselves:
idea.minimumSupported.version must be the marketing version that gradle.properties'
pluginSinceBuild pins.
java must be the JBR level the platform's JARs are compiled for - build.gradle.kts derives the
same value from the build number, and a wrong one fails the compile rather than the tests,
because javac --release validates the class-file version of everything on the classpath.
verify values are intellij-repository artifact ids, not marketing names: the keys of
PRODUCT_CODES in .github/scripts/ide-releases.js (ideaIU, rubymine, pycharmPY, webstorm, ...).
List a product only for versions JetBrains has published it for; they lag IDEA on new majors.
This affects verification only: test legs always build against IntelliJ IDEA.
An idea.additionalToTest version may be LATEST-EAP-SNAPSHOT. compose-legs.js resolves it once
per run, per product, to the newest EAP or RC build above the latest release, and every leg
gets that build. With no active pre-release, that product's legs are skipped with a notice.
Declaring anything twice is an error, not a second configuration: the generator fails naming
the duplicate, because every leg name has to be unique within a run. A second entry for a
version, or a product listed twice under one version, will stop the matrix before it runs.
beam.baseline must match the mise.toml pin, and must stay green. It is the newest supported
pair and the one every IDEA leg and the Windows leg run. beam.additional carries the rest,
either side of it, down to the oldest pair the runners can install: builds.hex.pm publishes
OTP for ubuntu-24.04 only from 24.3.4, so nothing below Elixir 1.11.4 can run.
beam.additional is a ratchet. continue-on-error means the version is NOT supported yet and its
leg is expected to fail; the workflow tolerates failure at every phase of that leg, not just
the tests, so an Elixir the toolchain or the quoter cannot handle still cannot block a merge.
Delete the flag once the leg is green - the version is then supported, and any later change
that breaks it fails the pipeline.
pull-request: true on a beam.additional pair makes pull requests test it; the nightly run on main
tests every pair. beam.baseline needs no mark, since every IDEA leg runs it. Pick the marked
pairs so that between them they cover each version-dependent behaviour that appears in a middle
Elixir and is gone again by the newest, not just the oldest and the newest.
continue-on-error on an idea entry makes that version's test and verification legs informational the
same way.
Check OTP support against https://elixir.hexdocs.pm/compatibility-and-deprecations.html, which
is patch-aware: 1.14 is '23 - 25 (and Erlang/OTP 26 from v1.14.5)'. Do NOT use otpVersions from
elixir-lang.github.com's src/content/elixir-versions to decide the range - it is per-MINOR,
misses OTP support added in a patch, and is published only from v1.15. Only the current
stable minor declares a recommendedOtp, and it is not the rule here either.
beam corpus lists the repositories whose .ex and .exs files the parser tests parse and quote on
that pair's leg, each as a GitHub https URL and a full commit SHA. For elixir-lang/elixir it is
the commit the pair's release tag points at (git ls-remote --tags). The build downloads each as
a codeload archive, so only GitHub repositories work, and it picks the corpus by Elixir alone,
so every pair of one Elixir must declare the same one.
A pair may also exist to cover an OTP major no other pair covers - ~75% of the swept BEAM surface
is Erlang and the chunk formats track OTP, not Elixir - so the same Elixir may appear twice with
different OTPs. Read by OTP major the pairs below are {24, 25, 26, 27, 28}, with 29 in the
baseline. Put a new Elixir on the newest OTP major it supports, so a failure is about the Elixir;
give a new OTP an Elixir that already has a green leg, so a failure is about the OTP.
